narrative:
The model estimated a 64% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, meaning it judged failure more likely than passing. Because your law school application was tied to that prediction, the application was rejected.

Ranked by influence, your third-year class standing was the most important factor. In your case it actually pushed the prediction toward passing, so it helped your case. The second most important factor, your undergraduate GPA, pushed toward failure: your 3.00 GPA was below the accepted-student average of 3.23. The third most important factor, your first-year class standing, also pushed slightly toward failure; your first-year decile of 6 matched the accepted-student average, but the model still treated it as a modest risk signal. Your third-year decile of 9 was the strongest factor overall and reduced the predicted failure risk, but it was not enough to offset the GPA and first-year signals.

Next, ask the admissions office for feedback and meet with an academic advisor. Focus on strengthening your academic record, especially through additional coursework or a post-baccalaureate program if needed. Consider retaking the LSAT only if practice scores show real improvement, and apply to programs that review applicants holistically.
